title: Sorting
html:
At this level sorting is a toolbox, not one algorithm: the shape of the data (binary, three-valued, small range, uniformly distributed, nearly sorted) decides the algorithm, and the partition / merge / counting ideas behind the sorts solve a whole family of problems on their own.

Sorting decision — choose the algorithm by asking three questions — how big is n, what do the values look like, and what is the cost of memory versus writes versus comparisons? — then pick the one whose guarantees match. The default (library sort) is right most of the time, but interview problems are built around the exceptions.

Which algorithm for which input

SituationBest choiceWhy
Binary array (two kinds of values)one partition pass (two pointers)O(n) time, O(1) space, no comparison sort needed
Array of three values (0/1/2)Dutch national flagone pass, three regions
Size n, values in a small range kcounting sortΘ(n + k), stable
Size n, values up to n² or n³radix sort (base n)O(d · n) with d = 2 or 3 passes
Uniformly distributed over a rangebucket sortexpected O(n) with k ≈ n buckets
Memory writes are expensive (flash, EEPROM)cycle sortminimum possible writes: each element written once
Only adjacent swaps allowedbubble sortit is the only one that moves elements one step at a time
Small n (≈ under 16)insertion sorttiny constants, adaptive, no recursion
Almost sorted inputinsertion sort / TimsortO(n + inversions)
Very little extra memoryheap sort / in-place quick sortO(1) or O(log n) auxiliary
Must be stable, general purposemerge sort / TimsortO(n log n) worst case, stable
Linked listmerge sortneeds no random access; O(1) extra space
Data on disk (external sorting)merge sort (k-way)sequential reads of sorted runs

The general-purpose comparison sorts are merge sort, heap sort and quick sort — all O(n log n) on average, each with a different weakness (extra memory, cache behaviour, worst case). Real libraries combine them into hybrids:

Timsort

Finds the natural runs already present in the data, extends short runs with insertion sort, then merges runs with merge sort using galloping. Stable, O(n) on sorted input, O(n log n) worst case.

Introsort

Quick sort that watches its recursion depth; when it exceeds 2 log₂ n it switches to heap sort (guaranteeing O(n log n)), and finishes small partitions with insertion sort. Unstable, in place.

Dual-pivot quick sort

Two pivots split each range into three parts; fewer comparisons and better cache use on random data than one pivot. Java uses it for primitive arrays, where stability does not matter.

Library callAlgorithmStable?
Python sorted(), list.sort()Timsort (merge policy refined to powersort in 3.11+)yes
Java Arrays.sort(int[]) (primitives)dual-pivot quick sortno (irrelevant for primitives)
Java Arrays.sort(Object[]), Collections.sort, List.sortTimsortyes
C++ std::sortintrosortno
C++ std::stable_sortmerge sort (buffer) / in-place merge if no memoryyes
C qsortimplementation-defined (glibc: merge sort, falling back to quick sort)not guaranteed
JavaScript Array.prototype.sortTimsort in V8 (stable required since ES2019)yes

Stable sort with a custom key in each language

A sort is stable when equal keys keep their input order. Sorting students by marks: with a stable sort, two students on 70 stay in the order they were entered. This matters for multi-key sorts (sort by name, then stable-sort by department gives “grouped by department, alphabetical inside”).

Pitfall

std::sort in C++ may reorder equal elements — the Asha/Meena order would be unspecified. Reach for std::stable_sort whenever ties matter. In JavaScript, sort() without a comparator converts elements to strings ([10, 9, 1].sort() → 1 10 9); always pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.

Tail call elimination in quick sort

Textbook quick sort recurses twice. The second call is a tail call — nothing happens after it returns — so it can be replaced by a loop that simply updates low and continues. That alone saves one frame per level, but the real win comes from choosing which side to recurse on.

Idea

Recurse on the smaller partition and loop on the larger one. The recursive call then always handles at most half the elements, so the recursion depth is bounded by log₂ n — even on adversarial input where plain quick sort would go n deep and overflow the stack. (Time is still O(n²) in the worst case; only the stack is now safe.)

Pitfall

The notes recursed with qsort(arr, l, p) after a Lomuto partition. The pivot is already in its final place at p, so the left call must be (l, p - 1); including p makes qsort(l, r) call itself with the same range when the pivot is the maximum — infinite recursion.

Time O(n log n) average, O(n²) worstSpace O(log n) stack — guaranteed
Key point

On this already-sorted input every partition is maximally unbalanced (p == high), so the naive version would recurse 16 levels deep. The smaller-side rule keeps the depth at 3 — and would keep it under 31 for any array that fits in memory. Combined with a randomised or median-of-three pivot this is what production quick sorts do.

Kth smallest element (quickselect)

Example

Input: arr = [10, 5, 30, 12], k = 2
Output: 10
Input: arr = [7, 10, 4, 3, 20, 15], k = 3
Output: 7

Idea

Sorting does more work than needed — we only want position k - 1. After one Lomuto partition the pivot sits at its final sorted index p. If p == k - 1 we are done; if p > k - 1 the answer is in the left part, otherwise in the right. Unlike quick sort we recurse into one side only, so the expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n).

Time O(n) expected, O(n²) worstSpace O(1)
Pitfall

Quickselect rearranges the array (copy it first if the caller needs the original) and has an O(n²) worst case with a bad pivot. A random pivot makes the worst case vanishingly unlikely; the median of medians pivot makes it a guaranteed O(n) at the price of a large constant. A size-k heap gives O(n log k) without modifying the input — better when k is tiny or the data streams in.

Minimum difference in an array

Example

Input: arr = [1, 8, 12, 5, 18]
Output: 3
Input: arr = [8, 15]
Output: 7
Input: arr = [10]
Output: INF

Idea

The two closest values in a set are neighbours once the array is sorted — any other pair has a sorted element between them, which is closer to both. So: sort, scan adjacent differences, take the minimum. O(n log n) instead of O(n²) for all pairs.

Time O(n log n)Space O(1) beyond the sort

Chocolate distribution problem

Example

Input: packets = [7, 3, 2, 4, 9, 12, 56], m = 3
Output: 2
Input: packets = [3, 4, 1, 9, 56, 7, 9, 12], m = 5
Output: 6

n packets with the given chocolate counts; m children each get exactly one packet. Minimise the difference between the largest and smallest packet handed out.

Idea

Sort. The m chosen packets should be consecutive in sorted order — if the chosen set had a gap, swapping an extreme element for the skipped one can only shrink the spread. So the answer is min over i of sorted[i + m - 1] - sorted[i]: a sliding window of width m.

Time O(n log n)Space O(1) beyond the sort
Key point

Minimum difference is the special case m = 2. Both problems share the lesson: sorting turns a “which pair / which subset” question into a scan of neighbours.

Sort an array with two types of elements

Three classic variants of the same problem — move every element of one type before every element of the other, in a single pass with O(1) space:

Example

Input: Segregate negatives and positives: [15, 18, -3, -2]
Output: -2 -3 18 15 (any order inside a group is accepted)
Input: Segregate even and odd: [15, 14, 13, 12]
Output: 12 14 13 15
Input: Sort a binary array: [0, 1, 1, 1, 0]
Output: 0 0 1 1 1

Idea

This is exactly Hoare's partition from quick sort with the predicate playing the role of “less than pivot”. i walks right over elements already of the left type, j walks left over elements already of the right type; when both stop they point at two misplaced elements — swap them. Each element is examined once.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

The Lomuto-style one-pass alternative — keep a boundary j; for each i, if arr[i] is left-type swap it to arr[j] and j++ — is shorter but does more swaps. Neither version is stable; if the relative order inside each group must be preserved you need the O(n)-space copy (or an O(n log n) stable partition).

Sort an array with three types (Dutch national flag)

Example

Input: Sort 0s, 1s and 2s: [0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2]
Output: 0 1 1 1 2 2
Input: Three-way partition around pivot 2: [2, 1, 2, 20, 10, 20, 1]
Output: 1 1 2 2 20 10 20
Input: Partition around range [5, 10]: [10, 5, 6, 3, 20, 9, 40]
Output: 3 5 6 10 9 40 20

Idea

Maintain three regions with two boundaries: [0, low) holds small values, [low, mid) holds middle values, (high, n-1] holds large values, and [mid, high] is unknown. Look at arr[mid]: small → swap with arr[low], advance both; middle → just advance mid; large → swap with arr[high] and shrink high (do not advance mid, the swapped-in element is unexamined). When mid passes high the unknown region is empty.

One routine, parameterised by the middle range [L, U], solves all three variants: 0/1/2 sorting is L = U = 1, three-way partitioning around a pivot is L = U = pivot, and partitioning around a range is the general case.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Advancing mid after swapping with high skips an element that was never looked at — the most common bug in this algorithm. Also note that the order inside the small and large groups is arbitrary (20 10 20 above); the notes' range example showed a stable order because it used three list comprehensions, which cost O(n) extra space.

Merge overlapping intervals

Example

Input: [[1, 3], [2, 4], [5, 7], [6, 8]]
Output: [1,4] [5,8]
Input: [[7, 9], [6, 10], [4, 5], [1, 3], [2, 4]]
Output: [1,5] [6,10]

Two intervals a and b overlap when a.start <= b.end and b.start <= a.end (they touch or cross). The naive approach repeatedly picks an interval, merges everything that overlaps it and deletes the absorbed ones — up to n passes of O(n²) work.

Idea

Sort by start. Walk through the sorted list keeping the last merged interval m. If the next interval starts at or before m.end, it overlaps m — extend m.end. Otherwise it starts a new merged interval. The key claim: a new interval can never overlap any earlier merged interval m' because x.start >= m.start > m'.end — once sorted, overlaps are only ever with the most recent one.

Time O(n log n)Space O(n) for the result (O(1) if merged in place)
Key point

Decide whether touching intervals ([1, 3] and [3, 5]) merge: the <= test above merges them; use < to keep them apart. The same sort-then-sweep handles insert interval, interval intersection and minimum meeting rooms (the next problem).

Meeting maximum guests

Example

Input: arrival = [900, 940], departure = [1000, 1030]
Output: 2
Input: arrival = [800, 700, 600, 500], departure = [840, 820, 830, 530]
Output: 3

Guest i is present from arrival[i] to departure[i] (times 0000–2359). Find the maximum number of guests present at the same time — the moment to hold a toast. Checking every minute against every guest is O(1440 · n); checking every arrival against every guest is O(n²).

Idea

Sort arrivals and departures separately and sweep through them as a merged sequence of events. An arrival increments the current count, a departure decrements it; the maximum count seen is the answer. Who arrived or left does not matter, only how many are present — which is why the two arrays may be sorted independently.

Time O(n log n)Space O(1) beyond the sorts
Key point

Because times are bounded (0..2359), a counting variant is O(n + 2360): add +1 at each arrival, -1 just after each departure in a 2360-slot array, then take the running maximum. This is the difference array trick, and it is the right answer when n is huge and the time range is small. The loop needs i to start at 1 with current = 1 because the first arrival is always the first event.

Counting sort

Counting sort — a Θ(n + k) non-comparison sort for values in a known range 0..k-1: count how many times each value occurs, convert the counts to starting positions, then place each element directly at its position.

Example

Input: arr = [1, 4, 4, 1, 0, 1], k = 5
Output: 0 1 1 1 4 4

That version only works when the value is the whole record. To sort students by marks (records with a key) you must move the original objects, which needs the stable formulation:

Time Θ(n + k)Space Θ(n + k)
  • Not comparison based — it beats the Ω(n log n) lower bound because it exploits the value range.
  • Stable when written with prefix sums and a right-to-left scan — this is what radix sort relies on.
  • Not in place: needs the count array and an output array.
  • Useless when k is much larger than n (sorting five values in 0..10⁹ would allocate a billion counters) — that is where radix sort takes over.
Pitfall

The notes' “updated solution” defined countingSort but then called the old Countingsort — a Python name-case slip that silently ran the wrong function. Case matters in identifiers in all four languages.

Cycle sort

Cycle sort — an in-place, unstable O(n²) sort that performs the minimum possible number of writes — every element is written at most once, directly into its final position. It is the algorithm of choice when writes are expensive (flash memory, EEPROM) or when you need the minimum number of swaps to sort an array.

Example

Input: arr = [30, 40, 50, 10, 20, 50]
Output: 10 20 30 40 50 50 (5 writes)

Idea

The final index of a value equals the number of elements smaller than it (plus the number of equal elements already placed). Take the element at position cs, count how many are smaller to find its destination, write it there and pick up the element that was there — follow this cycle of displacements until it returns to cs. Then move to cs + 1.

Time O(n²)Space O(1)
  • Worst and average case O(n²) comparisons — never use it for speed.
  • At most n - 1 writes in total, versus up to O(n²) for insertion or bubble sort.
  • In place, not stable.
  • The number of writes equals the minimum number of swaps needed to sort the array — the standard way to solve that interview question. When the values are a permutation of 0..n-1, the destination of x is simply x, no counting needed, and the whole sort becomes O(n).

Radix sort

Radix sort (LSD) — sort the numbers digit by digit, from the least significant digit to the most significant, using a stable counting sort for each digit. After processing the most significant digit the array is fully sorted.

Example

Input: arr = [319, 212, 6, 8, 100, 50]
Output: 6 8 50 100 212 319

Idea

Why LSD works: after sorting by the tens digit, numbers with equal tens digits are still in units-digit order because the pass is stable. Induction over the digits gives a fully sorted array after the last pass. Each pass is a counting sort with k = 10, so the total is O(d · (n + 10)) where d is the number of digits of the maximum.

Time O(d · (n + b)), b = baseSpace O(n + b)
Key point

Choosing the base. With b = n (not 10) a number up to n² has only d = 2 “digits”, so radix sort runs in O(2 · 2n) = O(n) — this is the “values up to n² or n³” row of the decision table. Radix sort is not comparison based, is stable, needs O(n) extra memory, and extends to negative numbers (offset or sort by sign first), fixed-length strings and floats (by their IEEE bit pattern). The notes' loop condition mx/exp > 1 was wrong: it skips the final pass when the maximum has a leading digit of 1 (e.g. mx = 100 would stop after the tens pass); mx // exp > 0 is correct.

Bucket sort

Bucket sort — scatter the elements into k buckets by value range, sort each bucket (insertion sort or any library sort), then gather the buckets in order. Expected O(n) when the input is uniformly distributed over the range and k ≈ n.

Typical inputs: integers uniformly spread over 1..10⁸ (too wide for counting sort, too many digits for radix), or floating-point numbers uniformly spread in [0, 1) where the bucket index is simply floor(k · x).

Example

Input: arr = [20, 88, 70, 85, 75, 95, 18, 82, 60], range 0..99, k = 5 buckets
Output: 18 20 60 70 75 82 85 88 95

Time O(n + k) expected, O(n log n) worstSpace O(n + k)
Pitfall

Bucket sort degrades to the cost of the inner sort when the data is skewed — if every value lands in one bucket you have just paid O(n) to run a regular sort. Pick the bucket function from the known distribution, not from hope. The notes' diagram listed 92 in the last bucket although the input contained 82; the example above is consistent.

Any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case — counting, radix and bucket sort escape this by not comparing.

Interview Q&A

Why do libraries use hybrid algorithms instead of plain quick sort or merge sort?

Each pure algorithm has a weakness: quick sort has an O(n²) worst case and deep recursion, merge sort needs O(n) extra memory and does unnecessary work on already-sorted data, insertion sort is quadratic but unbeatable for tiny arrays. Introsort (quick → heap on deep recursion → insertion on small parts) and Timsort (natural runs + insertion + merge) combine the strengths: guaranteed O(n log n), fast on real data, and — for Timsort — stability plus O(n) on sorted input.

Quickselect vs a heap for the kth smallest — when is each better?

Quickselect: expected O(n), O(1) space, but modifies the array and has an O(n²) worst case (fix with a random pivot). Min/max heap of size k: O(n log k), does not touch the input, works on a stream, and is better when k is small or when the data cannot be held in memory. For k near n/2 on in-memory data quickselect wins.

How can you sort in O(n)? Doesn't the lower bound forbid it?

The Ω(n log n) bound applies to comparison sorts. Counting, radix and bucket sort use the values themselves (as array indices or digit groups) and never compare two elements. They need extra assumptions — a small range, fixed-width keys, or a uniform distribution — and extra memory.

Why is the right-to-left scan needed for counting sort to be stable, and why does radix sort need stability?

After prefix sums, count[v] is the position just past the last slot for value v. Scanning the input from the right and decrementing before placing fills each value's slots from the back, so the last occurrence lands last — input order is preserved. Radix sort relies on this: when sorting by the tens digit, elements with equal tens digits must keep the units-digit order produced by the previous pass, otherwise the earlier passes are wasted.

Explain tail call elimination in quick sort. Does it fix the O(n²) worst case?

No — it fixes the stack, not the time. Replacing the second recursive call with a loop and always recursing on the smaller partition bounds the recursion depth by log₂ n, so even adversarial input cannot overflow the stack. The number of comparisons on that input is still quadratic; a randomised or median-of-three pivot is what makes the worst case unlikely.

Minimum number of swaps to sort an array — which sorting idea applies?

Cycle sort. Write each element directly to its sorted position (found by sorting a copy with indices, or by counting smaller elements), following cycles of displacement. Each cycle of length L needs L - 1 swaps, and the total over all cycles is the minimum. For a permutation of 0..n-1 the whole thing is O(n).
